checks.question: Would changing the primary outcome from pain relief at four weeks to pain relief at six months require reviewing the sample size assumptions?
checks.feedback: Relief percentages may change with follow-up time. The evidence and numerical assumptions should correspond to the outcome the trial will measure.

checks.question: Does the 40-percentage-point difference observed in the pilot have to become the target difference for the main trial?
checks.feedback: The pilot provides evidence for planning. The main trial uses a justified target difference of 30 points, taking account of the evidence, its uncertainty and clinical importance.

checks.question: With 90% power at a true 30-point difference, could the trial still fail to find a statistically significant difference?
checks.feedback: Under those assumptions, about 10 of every 100 repetitions would fail to detect the difference. These are false negatives.

checks.question: Can two trials with the same population relief probabilities and sample sizes produce different observed treatment differences?
checks.feedback: Different patients contribute different outcomes. This sampling variability produces different estimates even when the population assumptions remain unchanged.

checks.question: With standard-treatment relief kept at 30%, would achieving 90% power for a 20-point difference require more patients than achieving it for a 30-point difference?
checks.feedback: At a 5% Type I error probability, the requirement increases from 56 to 124 analyzable patients per group. Detecting a smaller difference with the same power requires more information.

checks.question: Under the normal approximation, would halving the target mean difference halve the required sample size?
checks.feedback: Halving the target difference increases the unrounded sample size requirement fourfold. A smaller difference is harder to distinguish from variation between patients.

checks.question: If 56 analyzable patients are needed per group and 5% loss is expected, is the recruitment target 118 patients in total?
checks.feedback: Dividing 56 by 0.95 and rounding upward gives 59 recruits per group. Two groups therefore require 118 recruits.

calculator.working: 56 / 0.95 = 58.947… Round upward to 59 per group. Then 2 × 59 = 118 in total.

checks.question: With 30 eligible and available patients each month and half consenting, would four months be enough to recruit 118 participants?
checks.feedback: Expected recruitment is 15 patients per month. Recruiting 118 would take approximately eight months at that rate.

checks.question: Would “The sample size was calculated in R” give another researcher enough information to reproduce the result?
checks.feedback: The report should identify the procedure, numerical inputs, relevant settings, software version and rounding. The calculation code makes these choices easier to check.

checks.question: Should the report explain why the calculation uses 60% versus 30% relief when the pilot observed 70% versus 30%?
checks.feedback: Both sets of percentages have a role. The report should identify the pilot observations and explain the assumptions selected for the main trial.

checks.question: Does reporting “118 participants” alone make clear how many outcomes are needed for analysis?
checks.feedback: The report should distinguish 56 analyzable patients from 59 recruits per group, giving totals of 112 and 118 respectively. It should also state the 5% expected-loss assumption.

checks.question: For an estimate of 20% with an interval from 15% to 25%, is the margin of error 5 percentage points?
checks.feedback: Each limit is 5 points from the estimate. The full interval width is 10 points.

calculator.working: The full width is 25 − 15 = 10 percentage points. Half of that width is 5 points.

checks.question: If the calculation targets an interval width of 4 score units, will every trial produce an interval no wider than 4 units?
checks.feedback: The calculation targets the expected width. With an assumed SD of 5, it requires 26 completed observations. Individual intervals vary because the sample SD varies between trials.

checks.question: Does this sleep dataset estimate the percentage with sleep difficulty within 2 percentage points at 95% confidence?
checks.feedback: The estimate is 40%, with an interval from 33.1% to 47.3%. The uncertainty extends approximately 7 points on either side. The report should also identify the population represented by the original trial and the 20 patients with missing sleep information.

calculator.working: The distances from the estimate to the limits are 40 − 33.1 = 6.9 points and 47.3 − 40 = 7.3 points.

checks.question: Do both 32 of 40 and 80 of 100 retained participants meet the rule requiring 80% observed retention and a lower 95% confidence limit above 70%?
checks.feedback: Both have 80% observed retention. Their lower 95% confidence limits are 65.2% and 71.1%, respectively. Only 80 of 100 meets both numerical criteria. Acceptable delivery is also required.

calculator.working: 32 / 40 × 100 = 80%. Also, 80 / 100 × 100 = 80%. The confidence limits are given in the pilot example above.

checks.question: With 100 analyzable patients per group, does the trial have at least 90% power at a true 30-point difference?
checks.feedback: Power exceeds 90% at 30 points. At the same sample size, it is approximately 83% at 20 points and 59% at 15 points.

checks.question: If several plausible assumptions give different sample sizes, is the smallest requirement sufficient reason to select that assumption?
checks.feedback: The choice needs supporting evidence and clinical reasoning. The report should show how plausible alternatives affect the required sample.

checks.question: Can statistically significant results from studies with low power exaggerate the treatment benefit?
checks.feedback: Among such studies, unusually large observed differences are more likely to reach statistical significance. Selecting only those results can give an inflated impression of benefit.

checks.question: If the simulated population difference is 30 points, does an interval from −5 to 25 points count toward confidence interval coverage?
checks.feedback: The interval excludes the known population difference of 30 points. Coverage counts intervals that contain that value.

checks.question: Should power estimated from 5,000 simulated trials match the planning formula exactly?
checks.feedback: Monte Carlo error causes variation between simulated batches. The planning approximation can also contribute to a difference between the results. More simulation repetitions reduce Monte Carlo error.

checks.question: With the same expected dropout percentages, can the estimated benefit depend on which patients are lost?
checks.feedback: If patients without relief are more likely to have missing outcomes in the novel-treatment group, its observed relief percentage can be inflated. In the selective-loss example, the estimated difference tends toward about 37 points instead of the true 30. This bias can reduce interval coverage and increase the percentage of statistically significant results.

checks.question: Does measuring each Parkinson patient both OFF and ON medication create paired observations?
checks.feedback: Each pair comes from the same person. Planning and analysis should account for the relationship between those measurements.

checks.question: If both independent primary outcomes must succeed and each has 90% power, is the probability of success on both also 90%?
checks.feedback: Under independence, the joint probability is 0.90 × 0.90 = 81%. Correlation between outcomes changes the calculation.

checks.question: Should a planned opportunity to stop early for benefit be included when calculating sample size?
checks.feedback: The analysis timing and stopping rules affect the trial’s statistical performance. They should be included in the planning procedure.

checks.question: Can researchers make a sample size calculation independently checkable without publishing individual patient records?
checks.feedback: The calculation can be documented through its inputs, methods, code and software. Supporting data can be shared through appropriate summaries or controlled access.

checks.question: Does a normal calculation giving 59 patients per group and a t-test calculation giving 60 show that one program is wrong?
checks.feedback: The procedures handle estimation of the SD differently. The comparison should establish which method and settings each program used.

checks.question: Is saving the random seed alone sufficient to reproduce a simulated batch exactly?
checks.feedback: The simulation algorithm, random-number generator and relevant software environment also need to be recorded.
